newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian court orders former SS major Hass freed.
newsitem.headline: Italian court orders former SS major Hass freed.

text.p: An Italian military judge ordered an 84-year-old former SS major suspected of involvement in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity to be released from house arrest on Thursday and said a civil court should now consider the case.

The ruling on Karl Hass, after a closed-door committal hearing, could create a legal nightmare. Another former SS officer, ex-captain Erich Priebke, is in preventive detention pending a retrial by a military court over the same atrocity.

Military prosecutor Antonino Intelisano had asked Thursday's hearing to charge Hass with complicity in multiple murder and put him on trial alongside Priebke over the SS massacre of 335 men and boys at the Ardeatine Caves outside Rome in March 1944.

The committal judge, Giuseppe Mazzi, instead accepted a petition from lawyers representing relatives of the victims that the case fell outside the jurisdiction of a military court and should be considered by the civilian judiciary.

"(Hass) is obviously satisfied with the judge's decision, because now he is a free man," his lawyer Stefano Maccioni told reporters. "Hass has no intention of leaving the country. He remains ready to collaborate with the authorities."

Priebke's lawyer, Velio Di Rezze, said the ruling marked the first step towards bringing both Hass and his client before a civil court. Civil plaintiffs confirmed that they intended to ask for the transfer of Priebke's case to a civil court.

Hass has been living under police supervision at a clinic where he is recovering from a fractured pelvis suffered last June when he tried to clamber over a hotel balcony and flee on the eve of testimony as a witness at Priebke's original trial.

Hass, whose home is in Switzerland, eventually testified from his hospital bed and it was that testimony which prompted prosecutors to seek his indictment on charges of complicity in multiple murder for the Ardeatine Caves massacre.

Priebke's trial ended in August in uproar, with the controversial verdict that he was guilty of multiple murder but could not be punished because of mitigating circumstances and the expiry of a statute of limitations.
Angry protesters laid siege to the military court, trapping Priebke and the judges inside in a stand-off lasting several hours which only ended when Priebke was re-arrested.
Italy's highest court, the Court of Cassation, quashed the verdict and ordered a new military trial for Priebke in October.

Judicial sources said Thursday's ruling incidcated Mazzi had agreed the crime was of a military nature but ruled that Hass should be tried in a civil court because he worked in a type of police, rather than military, office in wartime Rome.

Both Hass and Priebke have each admitted to shooting two of the victims at the Ardeatine caves. They say they were under military orders to participate and would have been killed themselves had they refused to take part.
Priebke was extradited to Italy from Argentina, where he had lived openly for almost 50 years, a year ago on November 21, 1995.
Germany has asked Italy to extradite Priebke and Hass for a war crimes trial there. The Italian legal process takes precedence over that request.
